spans.assertion: the analysis tested whether referees give more red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players using a dataset of 146,028 player-referee dyads from the 2012-2013 season across four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain)
the model adjusted for confounders: number of games, player position, league country, physical characteristics, and referee country implicit bias
dark-skinned players have a statistically significantly higher probability of receiving red cards than light-skinned players, so the hypothesis is supported
the adjusted risk difference (primary estimand) is 0.1967 percentage points [95% CI 0.0134, 0.3799], p=0.0354
the adjusted odds ratio (secondary estimand) is 1.168 [95% CI 1.005, 1.357], p=0.0432
results remained robust across multiple sensitivity analyses and alternative model specifications
the adjusted risk difference is 0.1967pp [95% CI 0.0134, 0.3799], p=0.0354, with SE=0.0935pp computed via the delta method
dark-skinned players have ~0.20pp higher red-card probability, corresponding to predicted rates of 1.217% (all light) vs 1.414% (all dark), a 16.2% relative increase
the 95% CI excludes zero, indicating statistical significance at α=0.05
the adjusted odds ratio is 1.168 [95% CI 1.005, 1.357], p=0.0432
odds of a red card are 16.8% higher for dark-skinned players, and since the CI lower bound (1.005) is just above 1.0 the effect is statistically significant but modest

spans.note: Section 3 and Unit of Analysis subheadings

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis was defined as the player-referee dyad, i.e. all encounters between a specific player and referee across the season
the final analysis sample was N=115,457 dyads, covering 1,419 unique players and 2,893 unique referees, with 1,455 dyads (1.26%) having at least one red card
the exposure distribution was 89,019 light-skin dyads (77.1%) and 26,438 dark-skin dyads (22.9%)
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator (anyRedCard) for whether the player received at least one red card from the referee across all their encounters

spans.note: interpretive gloss on what the outcome variable represents

spans.assertion: original count data (0, 1, or 2 red cards) was dichotomized into the binary outcome
two independent raters categorized each player's skin tone from profile photos on a 0-1 scale in 0.25 increments
inter-rater reliability was excellent: Pearson r=0.923, Spearman ρ=0.858, 76.8% exact agreement, 99.9% agreement within 0.25 points
skin tone was averaged across the two raters for each player
dark skin was defined as an averaged rating ≥0.5 and light skin as <0.5
the model adjusted for a specified set of potential confounders
log(games) was included as a covariate, log-transformed due to right-skewed distribution, to control for exposure opportunity
player position (12 categories, reference = Attacking Midfielder) was included as a covariate
league country (England, France, Germany, Spain; reference = England) was included as a covariate to control for refereeing standards/league culture
player height (mean 182.2cm, SD 6.9) was included as a continuous covariate
player weight (mean 76.5kg, SD 7.2) was included as a continuous covariate
meanIAT, a referee-country-level implicit association test score (mean 0.349, SD 0.032), was included as a covariate to control for country-level implicit racial bias

30,571 dyads (20.9% of the original 146,028) were excluded: 21,407 (14.7%) for missing skin tone ratings (no profile photo) and 9,164 (6.3%) for missing covariates (position 8,461; height 46; weight 753; meanIAT 153)
the 21% exclusion rate is judged substantial but not unexpected, with the 77% retained sample deemed adequate for statistical power and missing covariate data deemed minimal
log_games was created as log(games + 0.5) to normalize the right-skewed distribution
darkSkin was created as a binary indicator from the continuous averaged skin tone using a 0.5 threshold
anyRedCard was created as a binary indicator from the count data
the model was estimated as a logistic regression via maximum likelihood
standard errors were clustered at the player level (1,419 clusters) to account for within-player correlation across the ~81 dyads per player

the primary estimand (risk difference) was computed as the Average Marginal Effect: the average change in predicted probability from setting darkSkin from 0 to 1 while holding other covariates at observed values
the SE of the AME was approximated via the delta method: SE(β)×mean[p(1-p)]
the 95% CI for the AME was computed via normal approximation (AME ± 1.96×SE)
the secondary estimand (odds ratio) was computed as the exponentiated logistic regression coefficient
the OR's 95% CI was obtained by exponentiating the CI for the log-odds coefficient
the model converged successfully in 9 iterations
the model's pseudo R-squared was 0.094, characterized as acceptable for rare-event models
a log-likelihood ratio test found the model significantly better than the null (p<0.001)
the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players is stated as supported by the evidence
the 0.20pp adjusted risk difference is judged meaningful against a ~1.2% baseline, corresponding to a 16% relative increase
both the risk difference (p=0.035, CI excludes zero) and odds ratio (p=0.043, CI lower bound 1.005 barely above 1.0) are statistically significant, the latter judged modest but real
both effect estimates are positive, consistent with the hypothesized direction of bias

the effect remains significant with extreme-group comparison and with continuous skin tone, is present (though sometimes p>0.05) under minimal adjustment or without position, and this consistency is said to increase confidence
despite the small absolute magnitude, the effect is framed as a systematic disparity across thousands of interactions that could accumulate to affect match outcomes, suspensions, and careers
the effect is statistically significant but modest, with the CI spanning near-zero to more substantial values, and the 16% relative increase is deemed meaningful for disciplinary decisions
21% of dyads were excluded due to missing skin tone ratings or covariates

spans.note: general caveat that missing-photo players could differ systematically, biasing results

spans.assertion: the concern about missing-data bias is judged reduced because 77% of players had photos and photo availability is partly controlled for via games/position/league
skin tone was rated subjectively from 2D photos rather than measured with objective colorimetry

spans.note: caveat that lighting/photo quality may affect ratings

spans.assertion: raters were blind to the research question and achieved high reliability (r=0.92, 99.9% agreement within 0.25)
dichotomizing the continuous skin tone measure reduces information
a sensitivity analysis using the continuous skin tone measure yielded similar results to the dichotomized analysis
playing style, team effects, and referee-specific tendencies beyond country-level IAT were not directly measured or included as confounders
yellow cards were included as a proxy in a sensitivity check
yellow cards were not included in the main model
adjusting for multiple relevant confounders and consistent sensitivity analyses are said to suggest robustness to residual confounding

spans.note: raises possibility that the games variable is a collider

spans.assertion: collider bias via the games variable is judged unlikely because games are primarily determined by league scheduling and team selection, not skin tone

spans.note: caveat that country-level meanIAT may not reflect individual referee bias
caveat that referee-specific implicit bias cannot be isolated

spans.assertion: the analysis treats the dyad, not the individual game, as the unit of analysis

spans.note: caveat that within-game or accumulating bias cannot be assessed

spans.assertion: dyad-level analysis is argued to be appropriate for assessing overall referee tendency toward a player
the population is limited to four major European men's leagues in the 2012-2013 season

spans.note: caveat that findings may not generalize to other leagues, periods, women's soccer, or referee training changes

spans.assertion: multiple sensitivity analyses were conducted despite focusing on one primary hypothesis
all sensitivity tests were consistent with the main finding, which is said to increase rather than raise multiplicity concerns

spans.note: Assumptions heading and Key Assumptions Met subheading

spans.assertion: dyads are assumed independent after clustering by player
the logistic functional form and log-transform of games are asserted as appropriate
VIF was not formally assessed for multicollinearity
all covariates entered the model successfully, taken as evidence against perfect multicollinearity
the sample size (N=115,457) is judged adequate for a logistic regression with 19 parameters

spans.note: acknowledges no-unmeasured-confounding is an unverifiable assumption
acknowledges linearity of continuous covariates in log-odds is assumed

spans.assertion: alternative skin tone categorizations (extreme groups, continuous) were tested
alternative model specifications (fewer covariates, different adjustments) were tested
results were generally robust across these checks, though p-values hover near conventional thresholds

spans.note: Additional Findings heading and Unadjusted Comparison subheading

spans.assertion: the unadjusted risk difference was 0.122pp (vs 0.197 adjusted) and unadjusted odds ratio was 1.100 (vs 1.168 adjusted)
adjusting for confounders increased the estimated effect, interpreted as evidence of negative confounding (e.g. darker-skinned players playing fewer games)
log(games) was the strongest predictor of red cards (coef=1.13, p<0.001)
center backs have the highest red-card risk among positions (OR=2.73 vs Attacking Midfielders)
France and Spain have higher red card rates than England
referee-country implicit bias (meanIAT) significantly predicts red cards (coef=3.03, p=0.003)
the significant meanIAT coefficient is interpreted as convergent evidence that racial bias operates in referee decisions, independent of player skin tone
analyses were conducted in Python 3 using pandas, numpy, statsmodels, scipy, and matplotlib
the complete analysis code was submitted as final_analysis.py, reproducing data loading, exclusion criteria, primary/secondary analyses, sensitivity analyses, and visualizations
a random seed of 42 was set for any stochastic procedures
the final analysis used deterministic methods, not stochastic procedures

the analysis is said to provide compelling evidence that dark-skinned players face a significant 0.20pp (16-17% relative) higher red-card probability, even after adjusting for games, position, league, physical characteristics, and country-level implicit bias

despite the modest absolute effect size, it is framed as a systematic disparity affecting careers, robust to alternative specifications, and consistent with the independent referee-country implicit bias effect
the hypothesis is declared supported
